extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers in higher schools of literature; readers and scholars of comparative literary history
extracted.subtask_description: A series of didactic lectures surveying ancient and modern literature with emphasis on literature's influence on national character, language, and the conditions of literary excellence; intended as a textbook for higher-school instruction. Covers comparative history, criticism, and pedagogical questions for examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of literature on life and national character
rubrics_metrics.description: Literature should be judged by the influence it exerts on active life, the fate of nations, and the progressive character of ages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate works for how they shape morals, public affairs, and national disposition; the text uses the German and English revivals as examples of literature altering national feeling and practice. Anti-pattern: treating literature as merely private amusement with no public consequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of national (vernacular) language and national recollections
rubrics_metrics.description: A national literature must cultivate and preserve the national tongue and national recollections; the poetical art perpetuates a people's heroic and historical memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer writings that revive and embody vernacular strength, richness, and flexibility; study of foreign languages is useful only insofar as it polishes and enriches the native language. Anti-pattern: neglecting the mother tongue or blind imitation of foreign styles that obliterate national character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of literary activity with active life
rubrics_metrics.description: Men of letters must not be isolated from society; separation between literary classes and the rest of the nation is destructive to true national character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor authors and works engaging with public affairs and practical life; measure works by their social utility and capacity to enter public discourse. Anti-pattern: expecting authors to be impractical eccentrics whose writings have no influence beyond their own circle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual principles of imaginative composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Every work of imagination should proceed from (1) the expression of feelings common to all elevated minds and (2) patriotic feelings and associations peculiar to the people in whose language it is composed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess fiction/poetry by how well it balances universal human sentiment with specific national color and associations. Examples: national epics and popular songs that both touch human feeling and embody national memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of diverse social and mental faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: The formation of a national literary character requires the conjunction of varied faculties—philological learning, practical acumen, youthful enthusiasm, mature experience, and delicate sensibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value works that reflect a synthesis of critical learning, businesslike precision, imaginative energy, and social refinement. Anti-pattern: literature produced by a narrowly isolated class (e.g., only scholars or only court society) that lacks breadth and social resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, precision, and appropriateness of language as a criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Language—clear, precise, appropriate, and agreeable expression—is a principal mark by which we judge the polish and refinement of individuals and nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating prose and poetry, give weight to diction and expressive vehicle as indicators of intellectual culture; but beware of valuing surface diction over intrinsic moral or intellectual worth. Example: travelers revise opinions of a 'barbarous' people upon discovering a powerful, precise language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value and necessity of history and national tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: A plentiful store of national recollections, preserved in history and poetry, is indispensable to a nation's intellectual existence and long-term eminence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess literatures by their success in preserving and vivifying national history (historians like Livy/Tacitus, poets like Homer); anti-pattern: nations lacking writers who record and celebrate their past sink into oblivion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Durability and long-term influence as a measure of greatness
rubrics_metrics.description: The lasting influence of poets and philosophers (their effect over ages) is a better test of a nation's intellectual greatness than transient political or military achievements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer works whose ideas and aesthetic power persist and influence later ages (Homer, Plato) over works notable only for immediate political success (conquests, dynasties). Scoring note: emphasis on endurance and transmissibility of ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of literature for evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Literature, for the author's purposes, embraces poetry, narration/history, higher rational inquiry (philosophy), and written eloquence and wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include works across these genres when forming judgments about a nation's literary life; evaluate each by both intrinsic merits and collective contribution to culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of foreign languages as a means to improve the vernacular
rubrics_metrics.description: Study of foreign (including dead) languages must be rigorous and serves to sharpen perception of linguistic principles and to polish the native tongue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage comparative study and translation practice to enrich national literature; example: German writers improved their language through serious study of foreign idioms without abandoning their vernacular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candor and decisiveness in authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors who do not speak their minds freely and decidedly contribute to the contempt with which literature is sometimes regarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate authors favorably when they take clear positions and express them candidly; anti-pattern: evasive, overly ambiguous writing that avoids judgments and so diminishes the author's public authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical selectivity: winnowing original and influential works
rubrics_metrics.description: As a textbook, one should 'winnow the wheat from the chaff'—present what is original and influential, and not overload students with mediocre material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In instruction and anthologies, prioritize works that illuminate essential ideas and have demonstrable influence; use guided questions (as appended) to focus student attention on leading ideas. Scoring note: emphasize depth of understanding over volume of reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form must suit linguistic character (metrics and style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosodic and formal features (rhyme, alliteration, metre) must be adapted to the nature of the language; metrics effective in one tongue may be inappropriate in another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or evaluating verse, prefer forms native or well-suited to the language (e.g., alliteration/quantity vs rhyme differences discussed for German and French). Anti-pattern: mechanically importing foreign metres or banning traditional forms without regard to native idiom (Klopstock's attempted banishment of rhyme cited as error).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions required for a perfected national theatre
rubrics_metrics.description: A perfected national drama requires cultivated public taste, critical tradition, and access to great models (translations) rather than abrupt imitation or mere political patronage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess dramatic culture by presence of translations of exemplary plays (Shakespeare's effect in Germany), sustained critical work (Lessing), a public ready to receive and judge drama, and playwrights grounded in national language and sensibility. Anti-pattern: expecting theatre perfection without prior growth in taste and criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical engagement with philosophical doctrines in literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy affects literature strongly; philosophical tenets should be tested for practical and moral applicability rather than accepted as sectarian dogma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate literary works that incorporate philosophy by how thoughtfully they engage philosophical questions and by the practical moral value of the doctrines; beware of transient sectarian disputes that isolate philosophy from life. Example: Kant's moral and legal doctrines valued despite other errors.
